prs.title: Support empty higher-dimensional Euclidean pairwise sets
prs.head: be246bc9b2e9ac3b155a117ded22811a02534135
prs.body:
## Problem and change

`Euclidean(ndim > 1).pairwise_inner` and `cdist` flatten manifold axes with an inferred `-1` reshape. Empty point sets or an empty leading batch axis make that dimension ambiguous and raise instead of returning the correctly shaped empty pairwise result. Filtering away all matrix-valued or tensor-valued points therefore breaks these public operations.

Flatten only the trailing manifold axes explicitly. This preserves the point and broadcast batch axes, supports noncontiguous inputs, and keeps the existing calculations for nonempty inputs.

## Validation

- Unchanged upstream: **40 failures, 8 passing controls**.
- Both operations, float32/float64, two- and three-dimensional manifolds, empty left/right/both sets, broadcast empty sets, empty batch axes, and ordinary nonempty controls.
- Independent references broadcast the original manifold-shaped points and reduce products or vector norms. Output shapes, dtype, values, and gradients are checked with noncontiguous input views.
- New regressions plus existing Euclidean and manifold-basic suites: **2,159 passed, 310 skipped** on both Python 3.8/PyTorch 2.0.1 and Python 3.12/PyTorch 2.6.0. Ruff passes.
- [Reproducible original/candidate validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43849373630).

prs.title: Use a linear-time queue for synthetic tree generation
prs.head: 169899d014727842cceee661f3ba89e72ad78290
prs.body:
## Problem and change

The breadth-first tree generator removes each pending node with `list.pop(0)`. Every removal shifts the remaining entries, so wide trees spend quadratic work maintaining the traversal queue.

Use `collections.deque` and `popleft()` while preserving the existing FIFO traversal and random draw order.

## Validation and measured effect

- The existing dataset suite passes before and after the change: **32 passed** on both Python 3.8/PyTorch 2.0.1 and Python 3.12/PyTorch 2.6.0. Ruff passes.
- An end-to-end benchmark constructs real `StereographicTreeDataset` instances, including geometric sampling and sibling generation. Every output tensor, three indexed samples, the class count, and the final PyTorch RNG state have identical SHA-256 digests before and after the change.
- CPU, one thread, Python 3.12/PyTorch 2.6.0; medians of three runs with the same seed, dimension 2 and one sibling per node:

| Tree | Original | deque | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Binary, depth 8, 511 nodes | 0.1046 s | 0.1037 s | 1.01x |
| 100,000 children, depth 1, 100,001 nodes | 13.2191 s | 12.0607 s | 1.10x |
| 300,000 children, depth 1, 300,001 nodes | 43.6490 s | 36.5074 s | 1.20x |

The gain grows with queue width; small-tree generation is effectively unchanged in this measurement. These are complete CPU dataset-construction timings, not GPU or training-loop results.

[Reproducible original/candidate tests, benchmark, and output-equivalence checks](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43848030563).

prs.title: Respect curvature in Lorentz polar projection
prs.head: a790cf689ab6493917b5622d96c4dee93b007f93
prs.body:
## Problem and change

`lorentz.math.project_polar` scales the spatial coordinates by `sqrt(k)` but leaves the time coordinate unscaled. prs.title: Apply line-search stabilization only to committed steps
prs.head: a195aee07d4030ead58da6d54b9fb275bcaed6c6
prs.body:
## Problem and change

`RiemannianLineSearch(stabilize=...)` projects leaf parameters with gradients enabled, so an otherwise successful optimization step raises an in-place autograd error. The stabilization counter and projection also run for `no_step=True` and unsuccessful searches, even though neither commits an update. Manual stabilization can additionally leave the cached gradient tied to the point before projection.

Run scheduled stabilization only after a committed step, perform projection without recording autograd operations, and invalidate cached gradients after projection. The next search then evaluates its closure at the stabilized point.

## Validation

- Unchanged upstream: **28 failures, 4 passing controls**.
- Real Sphere and CanonicalStiefel parameters with Armijo/Wolfe searches and stabilization periods 1/2; stabilization-disabled controls retain their behavior.
- Preview and rejected searches leave parameters bitwise unchanged and do not advance the stabilization interval, with and without an outer `no_grad` context.
- Manual stabilization preserves trainable leaf parameters and the next update matches a fresh gradient at the projected point.
- New regressions plus existing line-search, unused-parameter, trial-cache, and retraction-derivative suites: **166 passed** on both Python 3.8/PyTorch 2.0.1 and Python 3.12/PyTorch 2.6.0. Ruff checks pass.
- [Reproducible original/candidate validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43844769239).

prs.title: Preserve caller gradients when initializing scaled manifolds
prs.head: fd3e256743cc73b9ca094e87312e4e3475f8c447
prs.body:
## Problem and change

Constructing `Scaled` currently calls `requires_grad_(False)` on the tensor returned by `as_tensor`. prs.title: Preserve spherical subspaces with dependent spanning vectors
prs.head: 27287337af8582524ebc603d8d9ff6ef675a97c5
prs.body:
## Problem and change

A sphere intersection/complement is defined by the span of the supplied columns. Reduced QR nevertheless completes dependent columns with arbitrary orthogonal directions. Repeated, zero, or redundant spanning vectors therefore change the manifold: intersections gain unwanted directions and complements lose valid directions. Checking the rank of the already-built projector cannot recover the intended subspace.

Construct the orthogonal projector from the basis and its pseudoinverse, and validate the intended dimension from the basis rank. This supports dependent and overcomplete spanning sets and rejects zero- or one-dimensional subspaces, where the continuous sphere is empty or consists of isolated points.

## Validation

- Unchanged upstream: **28 failures, 4 passing controls**.
- Repeated/zero columns and overcomplete bases are checked against analytically known projectors for intersection/complement constraints, Sphere/SphereExact, and float32/float64.
- Random samples and projected tangent vectors remain in the intended span; batches can contain different valid ranks.
- Empty complements retain the unconstrained sphere. Full-rank projectors and their gradients match the QR formulation and pass finite-difference gradient checks.
- New tests plus existing spherical subspace, manifold, and Riemannian SGD suites: **2,210 passed, 310 skipped**, on both Python 3.8/PyTorch 2.0.1 and Python 3.12/PyTorch 2.6.0. Ruff checks pass.
- [Reproducible original/candidate validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43842193798).

prs.title: Avoid square intermediates in canonical Stiefel gradients
prs.head: 784c5a0869fa7f0bda0af0f57749e17be1788e3a
prs.body:
## Problem and change

Canonical Stiefel gradient conversion currently evaluates `(x @ u.T) @ x`. For an `n × m` Stiefel point this creates an `n × n` intermediate, even when only a small number of orthogonal columns is needed.

Associate the same product as `x @ (u.T @ x)`, so the inner product is only `m × m`. The formula and its derivatives are unchanged, while work falls from order `n²m` to `nm²`. This targets gradient conversion directly and is independent of the Cayley-retraction optimization in #307.

## Validation

- **30 new tests pass on both unchanged upstream and the candidate**: rectangular and square points, float32/float64, broadcast and empty batches, non-contiguous inputs, finite-difference gradients, canonical-metric duality, and complete SGD/Adam training trajectories against the original formula.
- New tests plus existing canonical Stiefel, manifold, Riemannian SGD and Adam suites: **2,246 passed, 310 skipped**, on both Python 3.8/PyTorch 2.0.1 and Python 3.12/PyTorch 2.6.0. Ruff checks pass.
- [Reproducible tests, timings and allocation measurements](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43841173703).

## Measured effect

CPU, float64, PyTorch 2.6.0, one thread; gradient-conversion medians:

| Shape | Forward, before → after | Forward + backward, before → after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 32 × 32 | 0.00712 → 0.00699 ms | 0.06061 → 0.06052 ms |
| 256 × 16 | 0.04877 → 0.01055 ms | 0.23041 → 0.07144 ms |

prs.title: Keep Lorentz distances finite for large valid arguments
prs.head: 7f09fb9fc2e828ac5679824c8aaad75b4dd320c5
prs.body:
## Problem and change

The Lorentz distance kernel computes `acosh(x)` by squaring `x` before taking a square root. For valid finite float64 arguments above about `1.34e154`, that intermediate overflows even though the distance and its derivative are representable. For example, finite Lorentz exponential-map coordinates at distance 450 produce an infinite distance and non-finite gradients.

Evaluate the large-argument branch as `log(x) + log1p(sqrt(1 - 1/x²))`. Bound the inputs to both branches before selection so the inactive square cannot contaminate backward with overflow. The original regularized expression remains in use near the boundary, preserving its existing values and gradients at and below one.

## Validation

- The unchanged upstream fails **44 regressions**, while **14 controls pass**.
- Tests compare finite arguments through the largest float64 value against Python's `math.acosh` and an independently evaluated analytic derivative. They cover scalar and batched inputs.
- Boundary controls preserve values, gradients, and output dtype for float16, bfloat16, float32, and float64; finite-difference gradient checks cover both sides of the branch boundary.
- Public `expmap0(..., project=False)` → `dist0` and `dist` round trips cover distances corresponding to hyperbolic arguments 360, 450, and 600, three curvatures, both coordinate-axis positions, and `keepdim`; distances and derivatives remain finite.
- All new tests and existing Lorentz math, coordinates, axis, transport, and layer suites pass: **475 passed** on both Python 3.8/PyTorch 2.0.1 and Python 3.12/PyTorch 2.6.0. Ruff checks pass.
- [Reproducible baseline and candidate validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43839789228).

This change addresses the inverse-hyperbolic-cosine intermediate; the separate projection and general inner-product formulas are unchanged.

prs.title: Reuse coalesced row gradients in sparse optimizers
prs.head: 45f6f79216331db247fd22575ea95e5cc66c6b2d
prs.body:
## Problem and change

Sparse embedding gradients already contain one sorted row index and one dense value row per entry after coalescing. Both sparse optimizers nevertheless find the unique rows again, select those same rows from the sparse tensor, and materialize the result.

Add a shared row-extraction fast path for this common hybrid COO layout. Reuse the coalesced indices and copy the value rows directly. The copy preserves caller-owned gradients when momentum or Nesterov modifies its working buffer. Fully coordinate-sparse COO gradients retain the existing extraction path.

## Validation

- Real sparse Embedding backward/step sequences match PyTorch SGD and SparseAdam in float32 and float64. The Adam comparison uses a small positive epsilon in both implementations to isolate their differing epsilon placement.
- New tests plus all three existing sparse optimizer suites: **64 passed** on both Python 3.8/PyTorch 2.0.1 and Python 3.12/PyTorch 2.6.0. Ruff checks pass.

prs.head: d8898f1645ec66660631a0c52c0533220c9b97d0

## Problem and change

prs.head: d1ea20de7503e688f3b37b32b92845a9c101a221

Siegel inner products currently construct inverse matrices and multiply complete square matrices even though the result needs only a trace. This adds cubic work to both the bounded-domain and upper-half metrics.

Norm calculations reuse one scaled vector; the bounded model uses direct solves and avoids constructing either inverse. Upper-half cross products reuse the existing real inverse so that two complex factorizations do not make that path slower. The metric factor order, complex output dtype, broadcasting, and existing `keepdim` shape are preserved.

prs.title: Reduce intermediate products in Euclidean Stiefel exponential maps
prs.head: 78c37b66257412094c6cc6d54d58bd55c4044947

Take the first `m` exponential columns and compose their small right factor before applying the tall matrix. prs.title: Use low-rank Cayley solves for tall Stiefel matrices
prs.head: 2846064db5d6d637cf683167fc257507d301a8af

## Problem and change

When `2m < n`, apply the same Cayley transform through its rank-`2m` factors and the Woodbury identity. The solve is `2m x 2m`, and the implementation does not construct the dense `n x n` matrix. This covers `retr`, `transp_follow_retr`, and their combined operation. The existing dense path remains in use when `2m >= n`.

prs.title: Initialize sparse SGD momentum from the first tangent gradient
prs.head: a86617d9f6cd92dd723dabd40e6666e5362f0982
prs.body:
## Problem and change

Sparse SGD initializes its momentum buffer from the raw Euclidean gradient and immediately applies the recurrence again after converting the gradient to the manifold's tangent space. With momentum 0.9 and no dampening, the first Euclidean update is 1.9 times the expected SGD step. On a sphere, a normal component can also enter the first update.

Initialize the selected rows of a new parameter's momentum buffer from its first Riemannian gradient. Later sparse updates keep the existing lazy-row recurrence and checkpoint layout. A previously inactive row still follows that later recurrence; initialization is per parameter, not per row.

## Validation

Fifteen deterministic regressions cover real sparse embedding gradients with duplicate indices, four-step comparisons with native PyTorch SGD, float32/float64, momentum, dampening, Nesterov, maximize, independently calculated spherical retractions, delayed parameters, delayed rows, inactive-row preservation and checkpoint continuation.

The [exact-candidate workflow](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43816577279/job/133129886156) checks out this PR's commit, substitutes only the unchanged upstream implementation for the baseline, and restores the candidate for the passing run:

- Same new tests on unchanged upstream: **11 failed, 4 passed**.
- New regressions plus the complete existing sparse SGD, sparse Adam and dense first-momentum modules: **31 passed**. This retains the original 2,000-step Poincaré convergence tests.
- Changed-file Ruff and `git diff --check` pass.

Linux, Python 3.12 and PyTorch 2.6.0+cpu. GPU execution and the full repository suite were not run.

## Related work

#254 corrected first momentum initialization in dense `RiemannianSGD`; its changed files do not include `sparse_rsgd.py`. This addresses the separate sparse execution path. prs.title: Resolve omitted timestamps consistently in EKF and UKF
prs.head: 8cf3dc4d4cfdba7d049cac81fcf022c298a3b6a2
prs.body:
Fixes #519.

## Problem and change

When `t` is omitted, NLS reference-point selection uses the current system clock, but EKF and UKF pass `None` to the actual transition and observation methods. A time-dependent model can fail during prediction, or evaluate prediction at a different time from its Jacobian.

Resolve the default timestamp once at the start of each update and pass that value through the existing calculations. Copy the current clock so a later reset cannot invalidate a saved backward value. Explicit timestamps retain their existing behavior. The production change is one line in each filter.

## Validation

Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.5.1+cpu:

- New tests on unchanged main `298e9f0862cb228b0e8851b2616e682ccdca6a32`: **18 failed, 14 passed**.
- New tests plus existing EKF, UKF and dynamics suites: **50 passed**.
- Complete `python -m pytest -q`: **432 passed, 18 skipped**. The skips cover unavailable CUDA and the optional sparse backend.
- `git diff --check` passes.

The regressions compare actual posterior states and covariances with an independent scalar Kalman reference in float32/float64. They cover models that require a timestamp, models with their own `None` fallback, explicit overrides, repeated clock changes, time-independent controls and backward after resetting the model clock.

This targets the filters' direct model evaluations. #516 addresses saved timestamps inside NLS itself; #440 addresses independent-batch Jacobians. Neither contains this default-time resolution.

prs.title: Preserve independent EPnP directions when eigenvectors become complex
prs.head: 020e8f5d08a890d446bd42bfab58d381ade694a1
prs.body:
Closes #520.

## Problem

EPnP computes eigenvectors of the real symmetric Gram matrix with the general eigensolver, then discards their imaginary parts. Near repeated small eigenvalues, a complex-conjugate pair can become two identical real directions. The four selected vectors then have rank three, which can corrupt the pose estimate even for a valid scene with all points in front of the camera.

The five-point float32 example in #520 has mean reprojection error **481.06 px without refinement and 598.10 px with refinement** on the unchanged base. With this change, the errors are approximately **0.00070 px and 0.00015 px**, respectively.

## Change

Detect non-real selected eigenvectors and recompute only those batch members with the real symmetric eigensolver. Keep the existing real basis, reverse eigenvalue ordering and gather layout for ordinary members.

An unconditional eigensolver replacement was tested and rejected because another valid basis changed beta initialization and regressed two previously successful four-point refinements. This narrower fallback preserves those controls. Beta coefficient ordering and input broadcasting are unchanged.

## Validation

Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.5.1+cpu:

- The focused regression suite has **14 failures and 19 passing controls** on unchanged main; **33 pass** with the fix.
- Check basis rank and the invariant subspace against an independently constructed projective matrix and its SVD, across float32/float64, 4/5/9 points and multiple batch axes.
- Exercise public EPnP with and without refinement, the two successful four-point controls, mixed normal/affected batches, requested subspace widths, and finite nonzero gradients for scalar and mixed batches.
- A separate 96-scene comparison across 4/5/6/12 points and both dtypes reduces rank-deficient selections from **22 to 0**. No case with original reprojection error below 0.01 px exceeds 0.1 px after the fix. This is a measured regression sample, not a guarantee for every degenerate camera geometry.
- Complete repository suite: **433 passed, 18 skipped**. The skipped cases require unavailable CUDA or optional BAE dependencies.
- `git diff --check` passes.

All 329 prior PR diffs, 53 pre-existing fork branches, and all 134 reachable commits touching the PnP implementation were checked for an earlier equivalent change.

prs.body:

- Interior-draw controls retain their existing assignments.

prs.title: Preserve FastTriggs kernel ownership across copies and checkpoints
prs.head: d40393ed5234f358a55bd3edf643b4aa0cd23dad
prs.body:
Closes #527.

## Problem

FastTriggs captures its kernel only in a constructor-local lambda. A deep copy keeps that callable bound to the original kernel, so changing the original silently changes the copy's corrections. Parameters and buffers of a stateful kernel are also missing from the corrector's module tree, dtype/device conversion and state dictionary. Serializing an ordinary Huber corrector fails because the local lambda cannot be pickled.

This affects actual optimization: after copying a Huber corrector and changing the original kernel, a simple outlier-fitting Gauss–Newton step becomes approximately **0.08264** instead of the independent copy's expected **0.32258**.

## Change

Register the kernel as a normal child module and use a bound method to sum its output for the Jacobian callback. Preserve the correction equations and the existing `func(x)` callable behavior.

## Validation

Python 3.12.14 / PyTorch 2.5.1+cpu:

- Unchanged main: **13 failures and 6 passing controls**.
- Fixed focused suite: **19 passed**.
- Independent deep copies for Huber and Cauchy; full serialization round trips for Huber, Cauchy and Scale; stateful-kernel parameter/buffer restoration and float64 conversion.
- An actual Gauss–Newton optimization step agrees with its analytic weighted least-squares solution after the original kernel is mutated.
- Existing corrections agree with independent analytic kernel weights in float32 and float64.
- Complete repository suite: **419 passed, 18 skipped**. Skips require unavailable CUDA or optional BAE dependencies.
- `git diff --check` passes.

All 43 reachable historical commits affecting correctors, including intermediate source versions, retain the lambda capture. This does not change the inference-mode policy or Triggs' second-derivative handling.

prs.title: Keep xDeepFM norm gradients finite at zero residuals and filters
prs.head: a19e80dafb707cd6abb30de08b80da6dbf3040f1
prs.body:
### Description

xDeepFM expresses both RMSE and CIN Frobenius regularization as a square root of a sum of squares. At an exact fit or an all-zero CIN filter, the forward value is valid but the composed backward produces NaN gradients. An optimizer step can consequently corrupt otherwise finite model parameters.

Compute these objectives with `torch.linalg.vector_norm`, which selects a finite zero subgradient at the origin. Divide the residual norm by the square root of the element count to preserve RMSE. The CIN term still uses the Frobenius norm of the entire filter. Both occurrences of this zero-norm issue are handled together.

prs.title: Use the latest observed time in SLi-Rec preference fusion
prs.head: a9147aa957d9793832899e1285febfe95eae77a0
prs.body:
### Description

The adaptive preference-fusion gate reads `time_to_now[:, -1:]`, but the dataset left-aligns history and pads the remaining columns. Short histories therefore supply a padded zero instead of the interval since the latest real behavior. With two observations and a three-day gap, the gate receives `log(3)` at maximum length 2 and zero at maximum length 5.

Use the existing sequence length to gather the last observed time, and supply a neutral zero for an empty history. Full and truncated histories keep their existing temporal context. The correction changes the fusion feature only; checkpoint parameter shapes are unchanged.

Fixes #2456.

### Validation

[Independent validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/recommenders/actions/runs/43896904939) checks exact head `a9147aa957d9793832899e1285febfe95eae77a0` on Python 3.10/PyTorch 2.0.1 and Python 3.10–3.11/PyTorch 2.5.1:

- Patched model suite: **27 passed**.
- Native dataset tests cover short/full/truncated histories, maximum length one, and positive/negative sample groups. Additional cases cover mixed and empty masks and noncontiguous time tensors.
- Complete float32/float64 model predictions, parameter gradients and Adam updates match a separate row-wise reference that selects the last observed event.
- Black and `git diff --check` pass. Local Python 3.12.14/PyTorch 2.5.1 gives the same results.

### References and history

The [SLi-Rec paper, section 3.3](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2019/0585.pdf) uses temporal context to adapt preference fusion and evaluates the interval since a user's last behavior. This patch restores the observed interval as the fusion input.

prs.title: Select sequential checkpoints using the validation metric direction
prs.head: 201ca1ac15ae441749a7fad848cdb0a089f97a0d
prs.body:
### Description

The sequential trainer treats every validation metric as higher-is-better. Choosing `logloss` or `rmse` therefore saves the model with the largest error and can stop when that error decreases. A real SLi-Rec run selects epoch 3 (logloss 0.7067) although epoch 1 has the lowest observed error (0.7017).

Minimize the two supported error metrics and continue maximizing ranking/accuracy metrics. Initialize the comparison with the corresponding infinity so a valid zero score can establish the first checkpoint. Checkpoint selection and early-stopping patience use the same comparison. prs.title: Preserve RLRMC ratings for repeated pairs and low-memory prediction
prs.head: f74abf8dffada2f9f4b70286fd043aba4fd12b04
prs.body:
### Description

RLRMC trains on mean-centered ratings. Its low-memory prediction path subtracts the training mean, while its sparse path adds the mean only correctly for unique pairs. Repeated coordinates are combined by CSR construction, which accumulates their offsets and leaves some requested output entries unwritten. A factor score of 10 with training mean 3 consequently returns 7 in low-memory mode and `[16, -3]` for two identical pairs in sparse mode.

Restore the mean in both paths. Score sorted unique pairs with the existing sparse Numba kernel, then map the scores back to every original occurrence. Repeated and unsorted requests now preserve their order and multiplicity, and empty requests return an empty float64 array. This retains sparse scoring without gathering a dense factor array for every requested pair.

Fixes #2464.

### Validation

prs.title: Keep DKN item-to-item normalization finite in low precision
prs.head: eb6af96ae54feacc80b31fd3cb71869a55edc1ad
prs.body:
### Description

DKN item-to-item normalization squares article embeddings and applies its `1e-12` floor in the embedding dtype. In float16 the floor rounds to zero, so zero embeddings become NaN; small nonzero embeddings can also underflow during squaring. Native KCNN outputs then contaminate relation scores and the training loss, including under CPU float16 autocast.

Compute normalization in float32 for float16/bfloat16 embeddings, then return the original dtype. This preserves the squared-norm floor and zero-vector convention. Float32 and float64 keep the existing calculation exactly.

Fixes #2466.

### Validation

[Independent validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/recommenders/actions/runs/43902450955) checks exact head `eb6af96ae54feacc80b31fd3cb71869a55edc1ad` against unchanged staging:

- Python 3.10/PyTorch 2.0.1: **80 passed, 8 skipped** after the patch. One skip is the existing CUDA test; seven new float16 CPU cases require native linear/autocast capabilities absent from this version. An independent tiny operator probe confirms that limitation.
- Four dtypes and zero, small and ordinary embeddings are checked against a float64 vector-norm reference. Float32/float64 results additionally match the former expression exactly.
- Complete native KCNN/document-transform/relation-score paths run forward, backward and SGD updates with explicit half parameters and CPU half autocast. Scores, loss, gradients and updated parameters remain finite; nonzero cases verify that parameters actually change.

GeoIMC computes the same middle-factor matrix square root twice in every inference call, once for row features and once for column features. This repeated decomposition dominates the measured small-query cases.
